abstract: A systematic performance evaluation of attention-based deep-learning models for wavefront reconstruction in Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (SHWFS) systems is presented. While deep learning has been extensively applied to pyramid and focal-plane wavefront sensing, its application to standard SHWFS configurations remains relatively underexplored. A simulation dataset consisting of 3.5 million open-loop uncorrelated turbulent phase and image pairs modeled after the Subaru Telescope pupil was generated. The dataset spans four pupil-sampling cases (8$\times$8, 16$\times$16, 20$\times$20, and 32$\times$32 subapertures) under realistic conditions. A custom Vision Transformer (ViT) which incorporates features such as rotary positional embeddings, register tokens, and a cross-attention decoder, is benchmarked against a fully convolutional U-Net and a classical Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) linear reconstructor. The results show that the ViT architecture yields the lowest overall residual phase variance across all tested subaperture configurations, demonstrating a robust capability to model global spatial correlations and spot-to-spot cross-coupling across the pupil. While the U-Net performs competitively by capturing localized features, it exhibits $\sim1.5$ times more residual variance per mode than the ViT, which is relatively significant in high-order modes. This study represents a key step toward implementing attention-based models for high-order wavefront sensing and telemetry-assisted data reduction in next-generation instrument suites like ULTIMATE-Subaru.

title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health
authors: Chaitanya Pallerla, Dongyi Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.

title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current
authors: Tom Kimpson
publish: arXiv
abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.

title: Language models seek help despite guaranteed score losses in question answering
authors: Jiahao You, Ziye Jia, Chao Dong, Fuhui Zhou, Qihui Wu
publish: arXiv
abstract: At the highest waiting cost in a multiple-choice question-answering task, all 7 tested open-weight language models still consult an expert even though a correct expert answer earns fewer points than an incorrect independent answer. Pooling over expert accuracy and fixed-fee combinations gives help-seeking rates of 20.8% to 94.1% across models. We test 2,291 questions across 54 combinations of expert accuracy and consultation costs, comparing observed decisions with an expected-score baseline based on independently measured and calibrated model confidence. Help-seeking rates vary across conditions with the same expected consultation score. Fine-tuning reduces decision regret by 59% to 87% on held-out questions within the training range but increases inconsistency at matched expected consultation scores. In a separate task, external routing improves scores by 0.180 to 0.273 points per question with candidate answers held fixed.

title: Separating Genetic and Protein Evidence in Open Targets: An Auditable Re-ranking Study
authors: Ye Ye
publish: arXiv
abstract: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score, however, can be awkward to reuse for a narrower question such as which genes have direct evidence for disease risk or etiology. We examine this issue in Open Targets associations for Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD). Genetics-linked evidence and protein-oriented evidence are scored in separate channels and combined only at the end. In AD, the Open Targets overall top 20 contains 7 curated genetics-supported genes and 10 symptomatic pharmacology controls; the default late fusion contains 15 curated genes and no symptomatic controls. In PD, late fusion retains 13 curated genes and removes the 5 symptomatic controls present in the platform top 20. A genetics-only ranking reaches similar curated recall (14 genes in AD, 13 in PD), so most of the gain over the platform score comes from emphasizing genetic evidence; the protein channel mainly raises the number of tractable targets in the shortlist (from 9 to 12 in AD and from 8 to 10 in PD) without readmitting symptomatic controls. These results are stable across fusion weights from 0.35 to 0.75, perturbed protein-channel weights, and rule thresholds. An optional post-ranking rule further lowers high-clinical/low-genetic targets such as ACHE and GRIN1 without changing top-20 curated recall. The procedure is deterministic and uses public Open Targets fields. Because the component scores remain available, individual rank changes can be inspected and the ranking can be reproduced from the same data snapshot.

title: Global existence and large-time behavior of classical axisymmetric solutions to the two-dimensional viscous Saint-Venant equations and related models
authors: Xiangdi Huang, Muxi Lei, Weili Meng
publish: arXiv
abstract: In this paper, we study a two-dimensional compressible Navier--Stokes system with density-dependent viscosity in a disk, subject to the no-slip boundary condition. We consider both the symmetric viscous stress and the stress written in terms of the full velocity gradient. In each case the coefficients satisfy the BD relation $μ(ρ)=ρ^α$ and $λ(ρ)=2(α-1)ρ^α$. For every $1/2<α\le1$ and $γ>1$, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of classical solutions for arbitrarily large axisymmetric initial data with strictly positive density and possibly nonzero tangential velocity. Moreover, the density has upper and positive lower bounds independent of time, and the solution converges to the constant equilibrium. The two stresses give the same radial momentum equation, but require different estimates of the tangential velocity. The endpoint $α=1$, $γ=2$ includes the viscous shallow-water equations.

title: Selling Training Data
authors: Jingmin Huang, Wei Zhao, Renjie Zhong
publish: arXiv
abstract: This paper studies the sale of supplementary training dataset to improve predictive model. The buyer not only has private knowledge of its own dataset, but also can choose the way to merge these two datasets. This flexibility imposes a new constraint on the menu, requiring the buyer's total net utility be monotonic in the Blackwell order on private datasets. Given that, we show that a single posted price for a fully informative dataset is optimal in hypothesis testing, under differential virtual-value condition. The result extends to multi-class classification in which private datasets share a clean component but differ in how their labels are contaminated.

title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

title: Structure-Exploiting Hierarchical Retrieval for Long Narrative Documents: A Precision-Oriented Alternative to Learned Abstraction Trees
authors: Rohit Singh, Nathaniel Weems
publish: arXiv
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over book-length documents must locate a small, coherent set of passages inside tens of thousands of tokens. Flat dense retrieval ignores document structure; RAPTOR instead builds a hierarchy by recursively clustering and summarizing with a language model. We study a complementary design that exploits the native structure of a document: a two-level retriever that (i) selects chapters with a hybrid BM25+dense match over chapter recaps, (ii) runs a chapter-filtered dense search, and (iii) expands top passages into contiguous, section-aware spans under a token budget, plus content-hash-gated delta ingestion to keep the index cheap to update. We evaluate on five public-domain books (113 chapter-localization queries) and on QuALITY and NovelQA (200K+ token novels). In-house, we find a seed-stable precision/ranking tradeoff: with section expansion off, hierarchical retrieval returns a higher fraction of chunks from the correct chapter (+3.3pp, Wilcoxon p=0.014); with expansion on, ranking improves (MRR, p=0.040). Accuracy differences are not significant. On QuALITY, hierarchical retrieval beats flat top-k (81.0% vs 70.4%, p=0.0019) and matches the full article (p=0.74). On NovelQA, hierarchical and flat retrieval are statistically tied (55.7% vs 56.8%, p=0.24); hierarchy helps aggregation questions while flat wins on localized facts. Against a faithful RAPTOR baseline we find a complementary tradeoff, not superiority. Delta ingestion reuses 94 to 99.7% of embeddings on incremental edits. We make no claim of semantic chapter-boundary inference and scope claims to English narrative prose.

title: A Constrained Coupled Cluster Approach for Strongly Correlated Electrons
authors: Chenghan Li, Garnet K. -L. Chan
publish: arXiv
abstract: We introduce constrained coupled cluster (cCC), a general framework for imposing arbitrary physical constraints on conventional single-reference coupled cluster amplitudes without rederiving or replacing the underlying coupled cluster residual equations. As a first application, we derive a constraint from the spin-symmetry requirement for an exact wavefunction and demonstrate the resulting approach on strongly correlated problems. Across benchmark Hubbard models, nitrogen and chromium bond breaking, and iron--sulfur cluster spin gaps, the constraint strongly suppresses spin contamination, repairs qualitative failures of conventional coupled cluster, and often brings CCSDT, and in several cases CCSD, into quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization or high-accuracy density matrix renormalization group calculations. The derived constraint adds only a mean-field cost contraction to the coupled cluster calculation and is compatible with any cluster truncation. These results identify numerical constraints as a promising route for extending single-reference coupled cluster machinery into strongly correlated regimes conventionally associated with more complicated electronic structure methods.

title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
authors: Raullen Chai, Xinxin Fan
publish: arXiv
abstract: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to $mt=126$ (TII-228, $2{,}463$ CPU core-hours), with over $99\%$ of runtime spent harvesting weight-$(2t+1)$ codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves $1.0\text{-}1.5\text{ GB}$ of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. For $mt \le 145$, we pack all $mt-17 \le 128$ remaining syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices, share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$. Across four Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 144$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours) and TII-235 ($mt=144$, $4.30\text{ h}$ across ten L40S GPUs, $39.62$ GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), using $127$ of $128$ packed bits. These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters ($mt \ge 768$).

title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
authors: Cosmo Santoni
publish: arXiv
abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,μ\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

title: Constrained Online Selection with Predictions: Matroid Secretary, Knapsack, and Matching
authors: Hedyeh Beyhaghi, Tao Zixu He, Cameron Musco
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for constrained online selection problems, including the secretary problem under matroid and knapsack constraints, and the edge-weighted online bipartite matching problem with random vertex arrivals. In each, items arrive in a uniformly random order, and their values are revealed only on arrival. The goal is to select a set of items with nearly maximum total value, subject to the constraints (matroid, knapsack, or matching). In the learning-augmented setting, item value predictions are given in advance. We seek algorithms that are both consistent, in that accurate predictions lead to near-optimal selection, and robust, in that they obtain strong worst-case bounds even when predictions are inaccurate. Building on work of Fujii and Yoshida (2024) on the learning-augmented secretary problem, we study a method that follows the predicted optimum until an item with a large enough prediction error is observed. At that point, it reverts to running a worst-case competitive algorithm. We make a simple but critical modification: the first item with a large prediction error is selected with a carefully chosen probability. With this modification, we prove a general result, showing that if the underlying worst-case algorithm is $α$-competitive for $α\in(0,1]$, this approach achieves competitive ratio $\max\{\fracα{2(1+α)},\frac{1-ε}{1+ε}\}$, where $ε$ is the maximum relative error of any prediction. That is, the algorithm is perfectly consistent, achieving competitive ratio $1$ as $ε\to 0$, and robust up to a constant factor relative to the worst-case baseline. For all three problems we study, $α= 1/e$, and our result is the first to achieve consistency and constant-factor robustness. We hope that our general analysis framework can be applied to other learning-augmented online decision-making problems.

title: Friendship paradoxes in networks
authors: Eun Lee, Hang-Hyun Jo
publish: arXiv
abstract: Since Scott L. Feld's seminal paper entitled ``Why your friends have more friends than you do'' [Am.~J.~Sociol.~\textbf{96}, 1464 (1991)], the friendship paradox (FP) has been extensively studied in network science and related fields over the last decades. In this paper we survey the literature on the FP and its generalizations. We first introduce definitions and general results of the FPs defined in networks, and then overview their results on model networks. Empirical results using various social network data as well as applications to real-world problems, such as early detection of outbreaks and network sampling, are also summarized. Finally, we conclude by discussing several directions of possible future works.

title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
authors: Yanan Zhang, Shengqi Liu, Tao Zhang, Yidi Liu, Alan Tang, Hailong Chen, Yantao Jia
publish: arXiv
abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

title: Reward Blindness: A Theoretical Framework for Diagnosing Reinforcement Learning Reward Limitations in Text-to-SQL
authors: Lakshmi Muraleedharan Nair, Shiqi Huang, Fangyu Lo, Yihua Xu, Dingyan Shang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems let users without programming expertise query relational databases in natural language. Reinforcement learning has become the dominant way to train such systems, yet progress is still judged by a single number, execution accuracy, which counts correct queries but says nothing about which kinds of semantic error survive training. This paper develops a theoretical framework that examines text-to-SQL from the perspective of reward design. We introduce Reward Error Sensitivity, a measure of how strongly a reward function separates queries that contain a given error type from queries that do not, and prove a Reward Blindness theorem: when this sensitivity is zero, policy-gradient training carries no systematic signal for removing that error. Using fourteen published finegrained error signals for four text-to-SQL systems on the BIRD benchmark, we build error profiles and estimate sensitivities for common reward designs. Predicate and result-level errors are the most frequent, firing on up to 27 percent of queries, while structurally deep errors such as suboptimal joins persist at 5 to 12 percent. Each reward family has a distinct and predictable set of blind spots, and inexpensive database-level checks that need no language model calls detect 45 to 60 percent of semantic errors. Controlled training simulations confirm that executiononly reward leaves output-preserving errors untouched, whereas a signal-grounded reward removes them even when the detectors are noisy.

title: Local Limits and Structures of Nearest-Predecessor Random Graphs
authors: Xiaoyao Huang
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study the two-sided nearest-predecessor graph on $[n]$, where vertices arrive in a uniformly random order and each new vertex connects to its nearest earlier vertex on each side. We construct an infinite graph on $\mathbb{Z}$ from i.i.d. continuous insertion times and prove quenched Benjamini--Schramm convergence to it almost surely. The limit is almost surely one-ended and recurrent. We resolve an open problem of Ponomarenko by proving that the maximum degree is asymptotic in probability to $\log n/\log(3/2)$ as $n\to\infty$. We obtain the probability generating function and a CLT for the number of edges crossing the boundary of $[n]$ in the infinite limit. We also study the $K$-nearest-predecessor graph, in which each new vertex attaches to its $K$ nearest earlier vertices without regard to side. For every fixed $K\geq1$, we construct the infinite limit, prove almost sure quenched Benjamini--Schramm convergence, and show that it is almost surely connected, one-ended, and recurrent, as well as nonplanar when $K\geq2$.

title: Orthogonal lifting and amenability in ultrapowers
authors: Minghui Ma, Wenming Wu, Yifeng Ye
publish: arXiv
abstract: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a type $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor and let $ω$ be a free ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$. We prove that any two orthogonal separable amenable von Neumann subalgebras in the ultrapower $\mathcal{M}^ω$ admit orthogonal finite-dimensional lifts. In particular, two independent unitary operators in $\mathcal{M}^ω$ admit independent finite-spectrum representatives. We also show that the orthogonal lifting can fail whenever one of the subalgebras is nonamenable and Connes-embeddable.

title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
authors: Andrei Vlad Nicula, Kalp Shah, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Mihnea Andrei Bârsan, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jelínek, Chris Hoes, Remco Hogerwerf, Finn Govers, Storm Koper, Gerrit Janssen, Stef de Wildt, Alejandro Valverde Mahou
publish: arXiv
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

title: Does the Agent's Map Match the Territory? Architectural Claims in AI Agent Context Files and Their Fit with the Code
authors: Bachan Ghimire, Daniela Damian
publish: arXiv
abstract: AI coding agents start every session without memory of how a system is built. Developers fill this gap with context files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Agents treat these files as true, so it matters whether they match the code. We study two kinds of architectural claims that can be checked against a repository: path claims, which name folders and files, and dependency rules, which say what may import what. We check 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 context files in 3,346 open-source projects against the code and its history. About 5% of path claims point to paths we cannot find, but we estimate that only 2.2% are real errors, similar to READMEs (3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules behave differently: 33 of 184 (18%) were confirmed broken on the day they were written, usually by older code, and nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: their rules often describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. In an exploratory comparison of 7,480 commits, new rule breaks were rare. Agent-assisted commits broke rules about 1.8 times as often as other commits (0.29% vs. 0.16%), but with only 14 breaks this is not significant: an early signal, not evidence of a difference or of its absence. We used an LLM with human review at each step, and discuss what this offers and risks for mining studies.

title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
authors: Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou
publish: arXiv
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.

title: The XRISM view of the front and rear ejecta dynamics in Tycho's SNR
authors: L. Godinaud, A. Decourchelle, R. Giuffrida, T. Tanaka, C. Badenes, G. Ferrand, J. Ballet, T. Holland-Ashford, A. Bamba, B. J. Williams, T. Mizuno, F. Acero, J. Vink
publish: arXiv
abstract: We present a line-of-sight dynamics study of Tycho's supernova remnant (SNR) with XRISM/Resolve, based on five pointings obtained during the first two years of the mission. Thanks to a spectral resolution better than 5 eV, the spectra reveal a clear Doppler splitting of the Si, S, Ar, Ca and Fe emission lines towards the center of the remnant, allowing us to study the front and back sides of the shocked ejecta independently for the first time. Using a phenomenological Gaussian line model and a Bayesian fitting method, we analyze the broadband spectra of each pointing and of 149 individual pixels. We derive the dynamics and flux of the front and back sides for each element, as well as a global line broadening. The dynamics of Tycho's SNR are asymmetric, with the back side expanding faster than the front side for Si, S and Fe. We reveal a line-of-sight stratification of the elements, with Fe at lower velocities than Si and S. Si shows a strong front/back flux asymmetry, the front side being up to twice as bright as the back side in the northeastern part of the remnant. A similar but weaker asymmetry is found for S. For Fe, the flux ratio varies spatially, with either side dominating. These measurements allow us to reassess the average line-of-sight kinematics obtained at CCD resolution, which is affected by the flux asymmetry between the front and back sides and not only by a velocity asymmetry. Combining our line-of-sight velocities with Chandra proper motions, we reconstruct the three-dimensional dynamics of Tycho's SNR. Finally, we discuss the constraints these results set on the explosion model and the progenitor system.

title: Training-Free Interventions for Hallucination in Large Language Models
authors: Can Huang
publish: arXiv
abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, preparation cost, and the task on which a correction can be established. For activation steering, we distinguish estimating a subspace from applying a state-dependent edit and separate interventions on the prompt from those on the generated prefix. Published comparisons show why faithfulness to a source, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage must be measured separately. Applications in time-sensitive question answering, document synthesis, and visual grounding identify when source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation limits a reported gain.

title: Autonomous Multireference Quantum Chemistry with Artificial Intelligence Agents
authors: Younghwan Kim, Ming-Hsiu Hsieh, Ankit Mathanker, Arpan Choudhury, Joshua Zhou, Qiaohong Wang, Matthew R. Hermes, Laura Gagliardi
publish: arXiv
abstract: Accurately describing chemical reactions that involve strongly correlated electrons remains a major challenge in computational chemistry. Multireference electronic structure methods can address this challenge, but their application requires expert decisions that are di!cult to automate, particularly when the electronic structure changes as chemical bonds form and break. Here we introduce CASPER, an autonomously agentic workflow that performs multireference calculations along chemical reaction pathways. CASPER combines chemical knowledge, electronic structure calculations, and iterative assessment to identify chemically meaningful active spaces and maintain their consistency as bonds form and break. We demonstrate its capabilities on five transition-metal reactions, for which CASPER generates consistent multireference potential energy profiles with minimal human intervention. Importantly, in two reactions, CASPER identifies critical electronic-structure problems that an independent Claude session fails to recognize without the structured workflow. These include an electronic-state crossing and the exclusion of an orbital involved in bond breaking. Our results show the importance of combining language models with chemical knowledge and independent assessment of computational results. Beyond automating calculations, such agents have the potential to help researchers better understand the underlying physics and chemistry and open new opportunities for investigating complex chemical reactivity and generating high-quality quantum chemical data at scale.

title: Frobenius $2$-algebras and $R$-matrices
authors: Hibiki Shibuya, Yuji Terashima
publish: arXiv
abstract: In this paper, introducing Frobenius $2$-algebras, which are categorical generalizations of Frobenius algebras, we show that every Frobenius $2$-algebra determines an $R$-matrix satisfying the Yang-Baxter equation in the monoidal category of endomorphisms of its underlying object. Moreover, we illustrate this construction through three examples: a pair of objects in a braided monoidal category, a Hopf algebra with invertible antipode, and representations of the Heisenberg double of a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra. In particular, in the third example, we recover Kashaev's construction of the universal $R$-matrix. Thus, our construction provides a categorical generalization of Kashaev's construction.

title: The Optimal D.C. Bound Is Dominated by the Reciprocal of the Lovász Theta Number
authors: Yuqin Ao, Yong Xia
publish: arXiv
abstract: We resolve a question left open by Anstreicher and Burer (J. Global Optim. 33, 299--312, 2005). For the standard quadratic formulation of the stability number, we prove that the optimal difference-of-convex (D.C.) bound is at most the reciprocal of the Lovász theta number. The dominance is strict whenever the Lovász theta number is not exact.

title: Global strong solvability of the two-dimensional compressible Navier--Stokes equations for large initial data
authors: Jie Fan, Xiangdi Huang, Muxi Lei
publish: arXiv
abstract: In 1995, Kazhikhov and Vaigant introduced a two-dimensional barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes model with constant shear viscosity and bulk viscosity $λ(ρ)=ρ^β$. For $β>3$, they proved global existence of smooth solutions for arbitrarily large initial data with strictly positive density. More recently, Fan-Jiang-Li-Lü (arXiv:2611.20264, 2026) proved global strong solvability for every $β>1$ in bounded simply connected domains with Navier-slip boundary conditions. In this article, we prove global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to the Kazhikhov-Vaigant model on the torus $\mathbb{T}^2$ at the critical point $β=1$, for every $γ>1$ and arbitrarily large initial data allowing vacuum.

title: Parking Functions inspired by board games
authors: Alexander Clifton, Pamela E. Harris, Maryam Khaqan
publish: arXiv
abstract: We introduce two new parking schemes inspired by the classic board games Monopoly and backgammon. We consider a one-way street with $n$ parking spots and a queue of $n$ cars waiting to park. Each car has a preferred parking spot and enters in sequence to park. Under the Monopoly parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. Under the backgammon parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it bumps the already parked car out of that spot and takes its place. The bumped car then returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. A preference list is a parking function for a given parking scheme if all cars successfully park under that scheme. We prove that all preference lists are parking functions under both the Monopoly and backgammon parking schemes. However, the final parking order differs significantly between the two schemes. For a fixed permutation $π$, we provide a product formula for the number of Monopoly parking functions resulting in the outcome $π$. Analogously, we show that the number of backgammon parking functions with outcome $π$ is bounded below by $2^{n-1}$ and bounded above by the $n$-th Catalan number. We also obtain exact formulas involving Motzkin numbers for several families of outcomes. We define the displacement of a car as the absolute difference between the spot where a car ultimately parks and its preferred spot. Displacement multisets encode the displacements for cars with nonzero displacement. We provide formulas for the number of backgammon parking functions with a fixed displacement multiset of cardinality at most $2$, as well as for the number of Monopoly parking functions whose displacement multiset is a given singleton set. We conclude with some directions for further research.

title: Unveiling the Complex high-pressure phases of Sodium at the Melting Curve Minimum via Data-Drive Crystal Structure Prediction
authors: Zhenyu Wang, Chengqian Zhang, Xiaoyang Wang, Haiyang Niu, Jian Lv, Han Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Sodium exhibits a remarkable concentration of complex crystalline phases near its melting-curve minimum, yet the atomic arrangements of several experimentally observed phases remain unresolved. Here, we combine CALYPSO crystal structure prediction with Deep Potential models developed through concurrent learning to explore this structural landscape. Searches over more than 1.6 million configurations recover the previously reported $I4/m$ structure of $tI50$ and identify candidate atomic arrangements for $oC120$ and $aP90$, together with three additional low-enthalpy structures, $tI52$, $oP72$, and $oP92$. The proposed candidates reproduce key features of the experimentally indexed cell geometries. First-principles enthalpy calculations, Gibbs free-energy comparisons, and solid--liquid coexistence simulations reveal close competition among these structures and established sodium phases. Near the calculated reference melting minimum, $tI50$ is favored over $cI16$ and $oP8$, whereas $oC120$ and $aP90$ remain closely competitive, with their relative stability sensitive to model accuracy. These results provide testable structural models for unresolved experimental phases and reveal multiple closely competing low-enthalpy configurations near sodium's melting minimum

title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
authors: Josue Casco-Rodriguez, Nanda H. Krishna, Richard G. Baraniuk
publish: arXiv
abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

title: Logarithmic Potential and its Applications in Conformal Geometry
authors: Liming Liu, Shiguang Ma
publish: arXiv
abstract: We establish an intrinsic characterization of the end invariants $ν_i$ in the Chern--Gauss--Bonnet formula for complete, simply connected, locally conformally flat 4-manifolds with non-negative scalar curvature and $Q$-curvature non-negative outside a compact set. For each end $M_i$, we show that $ν_i$ is the cube root of its normalized asymptotic geodesic-ball volume growth: \[ ν_i=\left(\lim_{r\to\infty} \frac{V_g(B_r(p)\cap M_i)}{(π^2/2)r^4}\right)^{1/3}. \] This characterization uses only the Riemannian distance and volume of $g$; it is independent of the base point $p$, the choice of compact truncation of the end, and any conformal coordinates. The proof is based on asymptotic radial symmetry of the logarithmic potential outside a sparse $\mathscr{E}$-set, inspired by Hayman's work \cite{hayman1960slowly}, together with comparisons of radial lengths and geodesic distances.

title: G-Wave: Bit-to-Waveform Generation for Adaptive Wireless Communications
authors: Hanwen Zhang, Yunfang Leng, Zheng Shi, Bo Yuan, Zhenlin An, Haijian Sun
publish: arXiv
abstract: Wireless waveforms are traditionally hand-designed for general propagation conditions, rather than adapted to each specific environment. Existing neural transceivers seek such adaptation, but often rely on relatively simple architectures with limited long-range modeling capability. More expressive Transformer-based generative architectures are difficult to apply directly because wireless communication demands extremely accurate bit recovery, often with BER below 0.1%, while providing no ground-truth waveform supervision. To address these limitations, we introduce G-Wave, a channel-conditioned generative transceiver that directly synthesizes environment-adaptive physical time-domain waveforms from bits. G-Wave consists of Transformer-based transmitter and receiver models equipped with a multiscale architecture that combines long-range sequence modeling with fine-grained signal synthesis to meet the stringent precision required for communication. The two models are jointly optimized end-to-end using only bit-reconstruction error, allowing the waveform itself to be discovered without waveform labels. Across diverse 3GPP wireless environments, G-Wave achieves lower BER than the SOTA neural transceiver (DeepOFDM) and a strong conventional baseline (OFDM) under estimated channel information, reducing mean BER by 42.4% and 72.6%, respectively.

title: Sondheimer oscillations in Weyl semimetal films
authors: Lucas Méchet, Louis-Thomas Gendron, Ion Garate
publish: arXiv
abstract: In conducting films subject to an out-of-plane magnetic field, electron motion between the surfaces gives rise to conductance oscillations periodic in magnetic field, known as Sondheimer oscillations. While this size effect has been investigated in conventional metals, its dependence on the Berry curvature of topological materials remains less explored. In this work, we extend the semiclassical Boltzmann description of Sondheimer oscillations to type-I Weyl semimetal films. We account for the Berry curvature, the orbital magnetic moment and the effect of the Zeeman coupling on the Fermi wavevector and the electronic group velocity. The Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment generate a beating pattern and chirping in the Sondheimer oscillations. In the thick-film and thin-film regimes, we provide analytical expressions for the longitudinal conductivity, which highlight the interplay between electronic band topology and boundary-scattering in magnetotransport.

title: Trajectory Visibility at First Sight
authors: Mohammad Ali Abam, Mohammad Ghodsi, Seyed Mohammad Hussein Kazemi
publish: arXiv
abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, and let two moving entities $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ travel at constant (possibly distinct) speeds $v_q$ and $v_r$ along line-segment trajectories $τ_q$ and $τ_r$ inside $P$. We study the first-visibility time $ t^* = \min\bigl\{\,t \ge 0 \mid \overline{q(t)\,r(t)} \subseteq P\,\bigr\}, $ the earliest moment at which the segment joining $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ lies entirely within $P$. Prior work by Eades et al.~\cite{swat2020,eeades-phd} focused on the decision version of this question in a simple polygon. They gave a one-shot decision algorithm running in ${O}(n)$ time. For a stationary entity and a moving one, they gave a data structure with ${O}(n \log n)$ preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that answers decision queries in ${O}(\log n)$ time. For two moving entities, after ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ preprocessing time, they built a data structure of size ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ with ${O}(n^{3/4}\log^3 n)$ query time. Variants for polygonal domains with holes or when entities cross the boundary of $P$ lie beyond our scope. In this work, we go beyond decision to compute $t^*$ exactly under three models for a simple polygon $P$. When both trajectories are fixed in advance, we preprocess $P$ in ${O}(n)$ time and space and answer each query $(v_q, v_r)$ in ${O}(\log n)$ time. If one trajectory $τ_r$ is fixed while $τ_q$ is given as a query, we build a structure in ${O}(n \log n)$ time and space that computes $t^*$ in ${O}(\log^2 n)$ time per query. When neither trajectory is known in advance, we develop a data structure with ${O}(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ expected preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that achieves ${O}(n^{1/2}\,\text{polylog}(n))$ expected query time for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.

title: Grothendieck--Serre for quasi-split groups over two-dimensional regular local rings
authors: Ning Guo
publish: arXiv
abstract: We prove the Grothendieck--Serre conjecture for quasi-split reductive group schemes over two-dimensional regular local rings, that is, every generically trivial torsor under a quasi-split group scheme $G$ over a regular local ring $R$ of dimension two is trivial. Our main result is new when $R$ is ramified and generalizes Nisnevich's result by removing the assumption that the residue field is infinite. By formal patching of torsors and valuative criteria, we are reduced to showing a product formula when $G$ is semisimple and simply connected. Then, we take advantage of relative simple reflections and relative Bruhat decomposition to prove a generation by rank-one subgroups. The analysis on Dynkin diagrams with Galois actions reduces us to $\operatorname{SL}_2$ and three-dimensional $\operatorname{SU}$ factors. For the special unitary case, we treat Hermitian forms by using stabilizations and cancellation to finish the proof.

title: Semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash on H5N1 One Health questions
authors: Luizza Dalla Pria, Amelia l. Nelson, Renata Ivanek
publish: arXiv
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. We characterized the semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) on 15 H5N1 One Health questions sourced from social media discourse by adopting and extending a centroid-based evaluation framework. Each question was submitted 30 times and reformulated using five Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variants with 30 runs each, yielding 5,400 responses. Pairwise cosine similarity was computed on MPNet embeddings, with sensitivity analyses across three additional transformers. Statistical inference combined standard nonparametric tests (paired Wilcoxon and Friedman with Holm--Bonferroni correction) with inter-embedding agreement statistics (ICC(2,k) and Cronbach's $α$) introduced here as a methodological addition. Both models produced high mean consistency (0.93--0.97, rescaled to {[}0, 1{]}). GPT-5 showed reproducibility significantly higher than repeatability (W = 3.0, p = 0.0003), whereas for Gemini 3 Flash the two metrics were statistically indistinguishable (W = 42.0, p = 0.33). Differential Diagnosis ranked among the top two CoT framings for consistency in both models. The tested chatbots behave as semantically stable sources on H5N1 One Health questions, and the developed consistency evaluation framework is portable to other domains.

title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Xiatao Sun, Hao Wang, Ziyu Guo, Youheng Yao, Jingcheng Ni, Shenyuan Gao, Fengyu Yang, Renrui Zhang, Bangya Liu, Daniel Rakita
publish: arXiv
abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

title: A Positron Spectral Dip near 20 GV in Selected Orbital Projections of AMS-02 Data
authors: Yi Yang
publish: arXiv
abstract: We analyze more than a decade of public Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) data (2011-2021), matching daily electron and positron spectra to the orbital record on 3268 common dates. For each sky window we weight the spectra by the time the orbital zenith spends there and divide each rigidity bin by its all-date mean. At 16.6-22.8 GV, the normalized positron flux dips below its neighboring bins in several projections. At the Galactic center and the Crab, the positron dip exceeds the electron dip by $3.04\pm1.19$ and $3.57\pm1.22$ percentage points, respectively (statistical errors). A scan centered on 1177 Fermi-LAT catalog sources also finds dips at PKS~0301$-$243 and PKS~1424+240. At fixed rigidity, 13.8\% of trials that shift the spectra relative to the orbit produce a dip somewhere in the catalog at least as deep as the observed maximum. An isotropic intensity with the measured daily spectra reproduces every projection exactly. In a zenith pencil-beam model, direct positron annihilation on a common cold-electron column at the Galactic center and the Crab produces less than 0.10 percentage points of dip depth in either projection.

title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Sanjeev Arora
publish: arXiv
abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
